knowledge.text: Under the actual edit that replaced heating-only guidance with generalized heat/cool guidance and added a warning against using the final thermal appliance as a substitute, val:0015 gives a clear behavioral contrast. Parent P5 took tomato2 (P5:2), heated it at the microwave (P5:4), but then applied `cool tomato 2 with fridge 1` at the final fridge (P5:6), made an extra microwave round trip (P5:8-P5:9), and placed it only at P5:12, succeeding in 12 steps. Candidate Q5 took the same tomato (Q5:2), heated it while holding it at the microwave (Q5:4), opened the fridge and placed it directly (Q5:6-Q5:7), succeeding in 7 steps without the opposite cooling or redundant round trip. This supports the edit's clause against applying the opposite thermal transformation at the final receptacle once the required state is achieved, though this is one joint-edit pair.

The edit's direct hold-transformation pattern was followed in val:0012 and val:0014, but parent success and search detours limit causal attribution. In val:0012, candidate Q2 took tomato1 from countertop2 (Q2:11), cooled it at the open fridge (Q2:13), then opened the microwave and placed it (Q2:15-Q2:16), succeeding in 16 steps; parent P2 first moved the tomato into the microwave and closed it (P2:8-P2:9), later reopened, took it out (P2:16), cooled it at the fridge (P2:18), and finally placed it (P2:20), succeeding in 20 steps. In val:0014, both P4 and Q4 heated tomato2 at the microwave while holding it before moving it to the final fridge (P4:5/P4:7; Q4:7/Q4:10), and both succeeded (P4 7, Q4 10); Q4's extra steps came from an initial countertop/cabinet search detour rather than a thermal round trip. These pairs support direct transformation before placement and avoiding the final thermal appliance as a substitute, but the parent also sometimes succeeded and the edit was joint with search changes.

Under the actual missing-target search edit, val:0011 is a material parent-success/candidate-failure counterexample. Parent P1 reached countertop2 on its second action (P1:2), took plate1 (P1:3), cooled it at the fridge (P1:5), and placed it on countertop2 in 7 steps (P1:7). Candidate Q1 instead followed cabinets and drawers and its recorded 50-step trace contains no visit to countertop2 and no acquisition of a plate; it checked countertop1 at Q1:18 and later returned to cabinets after drawers, and ended still moving at Q1:50. Thus the new search guidance did not ensure coverage of the unvisited countertop where the parent found the target.

In val:0017 (put two creditcard in safe), the new numbered-instance search preference was associated with a large efficiency regression despite success. Candidate Q7 opened drawers1-10, took creditcard4 from drawer10 (Q7:20), then went to desk1 for creditcard2 (Q7:24) and placed both in safe (Q7:23, Q7:27), completing in 27 steps. Parent P7 went directly to dresser1, took creditcard1 (P7:2), placed it in safe (P7:5), then took creditcard2 from desk1 (P7:7) and placed it (P7:9), succeeding in 9 steps. Both found the required two creditcards; the material difference is search order and step cost, and the joint edit prevents isolating the numbered-instance clause.

In two other missing-target tasks the edit did not prevent step-limit failure or repeated visits to checked locations. In val:0013 (heat some apple and put it in diningtable), both P3 and Q3 reached 50 steps without acquiring an apple; Q3 cycled through cabinets1-6 and later countertop1, while P3 also repeatedly returned to the fridge, countertop1, cabinet1, and drawers. In val:0016 (put two book in desk), both also reached 50 steps; candidate Q6 reached bed1 only at Q6:50 and saw book1/book2 there but had no step left to take one, whereas P6's recorded trace ended at sidetable1. This shows the search guidance did not guarantee timely target discovery in either single- or multi-instance tasks; because no target was acquired, target locations elsewhere remain unknown.

In val:0012 and val:0014, candidates using the same missing-target search edit completed tasks after limited multi-location search. Q2 checked countertop1, fridge, and cabinets1-2 before finding tomato1 on countertop2 (Q2:10-Q2:11) and succeeded in 16 steps (Q2:16), versus P2's 20 steps (P2:20), whose extra steps included an initial microwave round trip (P2:8, P2:16). Q4 checked countertop1 and cabinet1 before finding tomato1 on countertop2 (Q4:3-Q4:4) and succeeded in 10 steps (Q4:10), versus P4's 7 steps (P4:7), which found tomato2 in the fridge immediately (P4:2). These pairs preserve successful target coverage and thermal placement, but the mixed step counts and open search order mean the edit's net efficiency effect is not isolated.
